text:
A southern California county spent more than $3m in a year on a security detail for its sheriff, Chad Bianco, a former Republican candidate for governor, and taxpayers footed the bill for items such as hotels rooms, travel and a $665 steak dinner.
A report from the Riverside county auditor-controller showed costs surged during the final months of Bianco’s gubernatorial campaign, peaking at $439,000 in April, and included flights, hotels, rental cars and meals for security personnel for campaign events.
The transactions cited in the report, which was first covered by the Riverside Press-Enterprise, include rooms at the Ritz Carlton in St Louis, where Bianco appeared on a podcast and a steak dinner in Los Angeles.
The high costs, including to support Bianco during his unsuccessful campaign, have raised concerns in the county.
“That amount of money spent in a given year is troubling,” Jose Medina, a county supervisor, told the Riverside Record. “It seems to be quite a very high figure.”
The sheriff’s office has pushed back against Medina’s criticism, arguing that the expenditures were necessary because of the death threats the sheriff had received. Don Sharp, the county undersheriff and Bianco’s chief of staff, said he was behind the decision to form and deploy the security detail.
Bianco’s “position, public visibility and the nature of the threats directed toward him create security concerns that extend beyond the walls” of his workplace, Sharp said in a statement.
“The security measures in place are based on safety considerations, not political disagreements. It is unfortunate that the need to protect an elected official has become a subject of political criticism,” Sharp said, adding that Medina “has repeatedly demonstrated his opposition to the sheriff”.
“Disagreements over policy and politics should never overshadow the fundamental responsibility to take threats against public officials seriously.”
Sharp also said that Bianco began receiving death threats during the pandemic, during which time he expressed opposition to state public health mandates, and that those threats “intensified over time, resulting in arrests both in California and out of state”.
Bianco came into the national spotlight in late 2020 when he criticized the approach of the California governor, Gavin Newsom, to Covid, and his “dictatorial attitude” toward Californians. He encouraged people to mask and practice social distancing, but called business closures and stay-at-home orders “ridiculous”.
He endorsed Donald Trump in 2024, stating: “I think it’s time to put a felon in the White House.”
In 2025, Bianco announced he would run for California governor as a Republican. During the primary, he came fourth and failed to advance to the general election.
This year Bianco also drew attention when he confiscated 650,000 ballots as part of an inquiry into specious allegations of fraud, an unprecedented move that the state supreme court determined violated election law. He was ordered to return the ballots.
Security costs began declining in June, before rising to $283,000 in September. In October, costs fell to $87,000 for the month.
